claim: JNK signaling plays a critical role in both tumor promotion and tumor suppression.
source: JNK signaling plays a critical role in both tumor promotion and tumor suppression.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 are clustered microRNAs that act as novel tumor-suppressor miRNAs.
source: Here, we identified clustered microRNAs (miRNAs) miR-306 and miR-79 as novel tumor-suppressor miRNAs that specifically eliminate JNK-activated tumors in Drosophila.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that these miRNAs suppress tumor growth in multiple models.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 specifically eliminate JNK-activated tumors in Drosophila.
source: Here, we identified clustered microRNAs (miRNAs) miR-306 and miR-79 as novel tumor-suppressor miRNAs that specifically eliminate JNK-activated tumors in Drosophila.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing suppression of various JNK-activated tumor models.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 show only a slight effect on normal tissue growth.
source: While showing only a slight effect on normal tissue growth, miR-306 and miR-79 strongly suppressed growth of multiple tumor models, including malignant tumors caused by Ras activation and cell polarity defects.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1M-Q showing minimal effect on wild-type clone size.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 strongly suppress growth of multiple tumor models including malignant tumors caused by Ras activation and cell polarity defects.
source: While showing only a slight effect on normal tissue growth, miR-306 and miR-79 strongly suppressed growth of multiple tumor models, including malignant tumors caused by Ras activation and cell polarity defects.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 3 showing tumor suppression in RasV12/dlg-/- and RasV12/lgl-/- models.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 commonly target the mRNA of E3 ubiquitin ligase ring finger protein 146 (RNF146).
source: Mechanistically, these miRNAs commonly target the mRNA of an E3 ubiquitin ligase ring finger protein 146 (RNF146).
evidence: Supported by dual-luciferase reporter assays and Western blot data in Figure 5.

claim: RNF146 promotes degradation of tankyrase (Tnks).
source: We found that RNF146 promotes degradation of tankyrase (Tnks), an ADP-ribose polymerase that promotes JNK activation in a noncanonical manner.
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments in Figure 6N-P showing reduced Tnks degradation when RNF146 is knocked down.

claim: Tankyrase (Tnks) is an ADP-ribose polymerase that promotes JNK activation in a noncanonical manner.
source: We found that RNF146 promotes degradation of tankyrase (Tnks), an ADP-ribose polymerase that promotes JNK activation in a noncanonical manner.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing JNK activation upon Tnks overexpression and by citations to previous studies.

claim: Downregulation of RNF146 by miR-306 and miR-79 leads to hyper-enhancement of JNK activation.
source: Thus, downregulation of RNF146 by miR-306 and miR-79 leads to hyper-enhancement of JNK activation.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased JNK activity when miR-306/79 are overexpressed or RNF146 is knocked down.

claim: JNK activity is essential for tumor growth.
source: Our data show that, while JNK activity is essential for tumor growth, elevation of miR-306 or miR-79 overactivate JNK signaling to the lethal level via noncanonical JNK pathway and thus eliminate tumors, providing a new miRNA-based strategy against cancer.
evidence: Supported by data showing that blocking JNK suppresses tumor growth.

claim: Elevation of miR-306 or miR-79 overactivates JNK signaling to lethal levels via noncanonical JNK pathway and eliminates tumors.
source: Our data show that, while JNK activity is essential for tumor growth, elevation of miR-306 or miR-79 overactivate JNK signaling to the lethal level via noncanonical JNK pathway and thus eliminate tumors, providing a new miRNA-based strategy against cancer.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing tumor elimination and increased cell death when these miRNAs are overexpressed.

claim: The c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway is an evolutionarily conserved mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase cascade that regulates both cell proliferation and cell death in normal development and cancer.
source: The c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway is an evolutionarily conserved mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase cascade that regulates both cell proliferation and cell death in normal development and cancer (Bode and Dong, 2007; Eferl and Wagner, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: JNK signaling can act as both tumor promoter and tumor suppressor depending on cellular contexts.
source: Indeed, JNK signaling can act as both tumor promoter and tumor suppressor depending on the cellular contexts (Bode and Dong, 2007; Bubici and Papa, 2014; Karin and Gallagher, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: JNK signaling is often activated in various types of cancers.
source: Crucially, JNK signaling is often activated in various types of cancers (Bubici and Papa, 2014; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drosophila provides a superb model for studying the genetic pathway of cellular signaling and has made great contributions to understanding the basic principle of tumor growth and progression.
source: Drosophila provides a superb model for studying the genetic pathway of cellular signaling and has made great contributions to understand the basic principle of tumor growth and progression (Enomoto et al., 2018; Tipping and Perrimon, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The best-studied model of Drosophila malignant tumor is generated by clones of cells overexpressing oncogenic Ras (RasV12) with simultaneous mutations in apicobasal polarity genes such as lethal giant larvae (lgl), scribble (scrib), or discs large (dlg) in the imaginal epithelium.
source: The best-studied model of Drosophila malignant tumor is generated by clones of cells overexpressing oncogenic Ras (RasV12) with simultaneous mutations in apicobasal polarity genes such as lethal giant larvae (lgl), scribble (scrib), or discs large (dlg) in the imaginal epithelium (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Pagliarini and Xu, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RasV12/polarity-deficient tumors activate JNK signaling and blocking JNK within the clones strongly suppresses their tumor growth.
source: These tumors activate JNK signaling and blocking JNK within the clones strongly suppresses their tumor growth (Igaki et al., 2006; Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006), indicating that JNK acts as a pro-tumor signaling in these malignant tumors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: JNK acts as a pro-tumor signaling in RasV12/polarity-deficient malignant tumors.
source: These tumors activate JNK signaling and blocking JNK within the clones strongly suppresses their tumor growth (Igaki et al., 2006; Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006), indicating that JNK acts as a pro-tumor signaling in these malignant tumors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking JNK suppresses tumor growth, supported by citations.

claim: Clones of cells overexpressing the oncogene Src in the imaginal discs activate JNK signaling and blocking JNK in these clones results in enhanced overgrowth.
source: Conversely, clones of cells overexpressing the oncogene Src in the imaginal discs activate JNK signaling and blocking JNK in these clones results in an enhanced overgrowth (Enomoto and Igaki, 2013), indicating that JNK negatively regulates Src-induced tumor growth.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: JNK negatively regulates Src-induced tumor growth.
source: Conversely, clones of cells overexpressing the oncogene Src in the imaginal discs activate JNK signaling and blocking JNK in these clones results in an enhanced overgrowth (Enomoto and Igaki, 2013), indicating that JNK negatively regulates Src-induced tumor growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking JNK enhances overgrowth, supported by a citation.

claim: Clones of cells mutant for scrib or dlg in the imaginal discs are eliminated by apoptosis when surrounded by wild-type cells.
source: Similarly, although clones of cells mutant for scrib or dlg in the imaginal discs are eliminated by apoptosis when surrounded by wild-type cells, blocking JNK in these clones suppresses elimination and causes tumorous overgrowth (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Igaki et al., 2009), indicating that JNK acts as antitumor signaling in these mutant clones.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Blocking JNK in scrib or dlg mutant clones suppresses elimination and causes tumorous overgrowth.
source: Similarly, although clones of cells mutant for scrib or dlg in the imaginal discs are eliminated by apoptosis when surrounded by wild-type cells, blocking JNK in these clones suppresses elimination and causes tumorous overgrowth (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Igaki et al., 2009), indicating that JNK acts as antitumor signaling in these mutant clones.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: JNK acts as antitumor signaling in scrib or dlg mutant clones.
source: Similarly, although clones of cells mutant for scrib or dlg in the imaginal discs are eliminated by apoptosis when surrounded by wild-type cells, blocking JNK in these clones suppresses elimination and causes tumorous overgrowth (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Igaki et al., 2009), indicating that JNK acts as antitumor signaling in these mutant clones.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking JNK causes overgrowth, supported by citations.

claim: miRNAs are a group of small noncoding RNAs that suppress target gene expression by mRNA degradation or translational repression.
source: miRNAs are a group of small noncoding RNAs that suppress target gene expression by mRNA degradation or translational repression and have been proposed to be potent targets for cancer therapy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA function.

claim: Several cancer-targeted miRNA drugs have entered clinical trials in recent years.
source: Indeed, several cancer-targeted miRNA drugs have entered clinical trials in recent years.
evidence: This statement is supported by subsequent examples with citations.

claim: MRX34, a miRNA mimic drug developed from tumor-suppressor miR-34a, is the first miRNA-based anticancer drug that has entered phase I clinical trials for patients with advanced solid tumors.
source: For instance, MRX34, a miRNA mimic drug developed from the tumor-suppressor miR-34a, is the first miRNA-based anticancer drug that has entered phase I clinical trials for patients with advanced solid tumors (Beg et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MesomiR-1, a miR-16 mimic miRNA that targets EGFR, has entered phase I trial for the treatment of thoracic cancers.
source: In addition, MesomiR-1, a miR-16 mimic miRNA that targets EGFR, has entered phase I trial for the treatment of thoracic cancers (Reid et al., 2013; van Zandwijk et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The conserved miRNA let-7 targets a transcription factor chinmo and suppresses tumor growth caused by polyhomeotic mutations in Drosophila.
source: Indeed, in Drosophila, the conserved miRNA let-7 targets a transcription factor chinmo and thus suppresses tumor growth caused by polyhomeotic mutations (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: miR-8 acts as a tumor suppressor against Notch-induced Drosophila tumors by directly inhibiting the Notch ligand Serrate.
source: In addition, miR-8 acts as a tumor suppressor against Notch-induced Drosophila tumors by directly inhibiting the Notch ligand Serrate (Vallejo et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of miR-7, miR-79, miR-252, miR-276a, miR-276b, miR-282, miR-306, miR-310, miR-317, miR-981, miR-988, or the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster in RasV12/dlg-/- clones dramatically suppressed tumor growth.
source: We found that overexpression of miR-7, miR-79, miR-252, miR-276a, miR-276b, miR-282, miR-306, miR-310, miR-317, miR-981, miR-988, or the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster in RasV12/dlg-/- clones dramatically suppressed tumor growth (Figure 1C–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, R, S, T, W, Y, Z, AC, and AE, quantified in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1AI).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of miR-305, miR-995, or the miR-13a/13b-1/2c cluster mildly suppressed RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth.
source: In addition, overexpression of miR-305, miR-995, or the miR-13a/13b-1/2c cluster mildly suppressed RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K, X and AF, quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1AI).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 dramatically inhibited RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth.
source: Notably, overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 dramatically inhibited RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth (Figure 1E–G, compare to Figure 1D, quantified in Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 was sufficient to rescue the reduced pupation rate caused by RasV12/dlg-/- tumors in the eye-antennal discs.
source: In addition, overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 was sufficient to rescue the reduced pupation rate and animal lethality caused by RasV12/dlg-/- tumors in the eye-antennal discs (Figure 1I and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 was sufficient to rescue animal lethality caused by RasV12/dlg-/- tumors in the eye-antennal discs.
source: In addition, overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 was sufficient to rescue the reduced pupation rate and animal lethality caused by RasV12/dlg-/- tumors in the eye-antennal discs (Figure 1I and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Overexpression of miR-79 suppressed tumor growth caused by coexpression of RasV12 and lgl-RNAi in Drosophila wing discs.
source: A pervious study in Drosophila wing discs showed that overexpression of miR-79 suppressed tumor growth caused by coexpression of RasV12 and lgl-RNAi via unknown mechanisms (Shu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 strongly suppressed growth of RasV12/lgl-/- tumors in the eye-antennal discs.
source: Similarly, we found that overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 strongly suppressed growth of RasV12/lgl-/- tumors in the eye-antennal discs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D, quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 alone only slightly reduced clone size compared to wild-type.
source: Importantly, overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 alone only slightly reduced clone size compared to wild-type (Figure 1M–P, quantified in Figure 1Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M-Q.

claim: Expression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 in RasV12/dlg-/- or RasV12/lgl-/- tumor clones significantly increased the number of dying cells.
source: Immunostaining of RasV12/dlg-/- or RasV12/lgl-/- tumors with anti-cleaved DCP-1 antibody revealed that expression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 in tumor clones significantly increased the number of dying cells (Figure 2A–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D, quantified in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Blocking cell death in tumor clones by overexpressing the caspase inhibitor baculovirus p35 canceled the tumor-suppressive activity of miR-306 or miR-79.
source: In addition, blocking cell death in tumor clones by overexpressing the caspase inhibitor baculovirus p35 canceled the tumor-suppressive activity of miR-306 or miR-79, while p35 overexpression alone did not affect growth of normal tissues or RasV12/dlg-/- tumors (Figure 2G–N, quantified in Figure 2O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-O.

claim: p35 overexpression alone did not affect growth of normal tissues or RasV12/dlg-/- tumors.
source: In addition, blocking cell death in tumor clones by overexpressing the caspase inhibitor baculovirus p35 canceled the tumor-suppressive activity of miR-306 or miR-79, while p35 overexpression alone did not affect growth of normal tissues or RasV12/dlg-/- tumors (Figure 2G–N, quantified in Figure 2O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-O.

claim: The miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 suppresses tumor growth by inducing cell death.
source: These data indicate that the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 suppresses tumor growth by inducing cell death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking cell death cancels tumor suppression.

claim: Overexpression of miR-306, miR-79, or the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster alone did not cause cell death in normal tissue.
source: Importantly, overexpression of these miRNAs alone did not cause cell death in normal tissue (Figure 2P–S, quantified in Figure 2T), suggesting that miR-306 or miR-79 cooperates with a putative tumor-specific signaling activated in RasV12/dlg-/- or RasV12/lgl-/- tumors to induce synthetic lethality.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2P-T.

claim: miR-306 or miR-79 cooperates with a putative tumor-specific signaling activated in RasV12/dlg-/- or RasV12/lgl-/- tumors to induce synthetic lethality.
source: Importantly, overexpression of these miRNAs alone did not cause cell death in normal tissue (Figure 2P–S, quantified in Figure 2T), suggesting that miR-306 or miR-79 cooperates with a putative tumor-specific signaling activated in RasV12/dlg-/- or RasV12/lgl-/- tumors to induce synthetic lethality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these miRNAs only induce death in tumor cells, not normal cells.

claim: Overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 in RasV12-expressing clones did not affect their growth.
source: Overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 in RasV12-expresing clones did not affect their growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), indicating that Ras signaling does not cooperate with these miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Ras signaling does not cooperate with miR-306, miR-79, or the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster.
source: Overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 in RasV12-expresing clones did not affect their growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), indicating that Ras signaling does not cooperate with these miRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these miRNAs do not affect RasV12 clone growth.

claim: Overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 in dlg-/- clones significantly reduced their clone size.
source: Notably, overexpression of these miRNAs in dlg-/- clones significantly reduced their clone size (Figure 3A–E, quantified in Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-F.

claim: Blocking cell death by overexpression of p35 canceled the ability of miR-306, miR-79, or the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster to reduce dlg-/- clone size.
source: In addition, blocking cell death by overexpression of p35 canceled the ability of these miRNAs to reduce dlg-/- clone size (Figure 3G–O, quantified in Figure 3P), suggesting that these miRNAs block dlg-/- clone growth by promoting cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G-P.

claim: miR-306, miR-79, or the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster block dlg-/- clone growth by promoting cell death.
source: In addition, blocking cell death by overexpression of p35 canceled the ability of these miRNAs to reduce dlg-/- clone size (Figure 3G–O, quantified in Figure 3P), suggesting that these miRNAs block dlg-/- clone growth by promoting cell death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking cell death rescues clone size.

claim: miR-306 or miR-79 cooperates with loss of cell polarity to induce synthetic lethality.
source: These data show that miR-306 or miR-79 cooperates with loss of cell polarity to induce synthetic lethality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these miRNAs reduce dlg-/- clone size by promoting cell death.

claim: Clones of cells mutant for cell polarity genes such as dlg activate JNK signaling via the Drosophila tumor necrosis factor (TNF) Eiger.
source: It has been shown that clones of cells mutant for cell polarity genes such as dlg activate JNK signaling via the Drosophila tumor necrosis factor (TNF) Eiger (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Igaki et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 alone moderately activated JNK signaling in the eye-antennal discs.
source: We found that overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 alone moderately activated JNK signaling in the eye-antennal discs, as visualized by anti-p-JNK antibody staining and the puc-LacZ reporter (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 in the eyes using the GMR-Gal4 driver caused JNK activation.
source: In addition, Western blot analysis with anti-p-JNK antibody revealed that overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 in the eyes using the GMR-Gal4 driver caused JNK activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 alone in the eyes had no significant effect on eye morphology.
source: Notably, although overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 alone in the eyes had no significant effect on eye morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I–K, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 2L), they dramatically enhanced the reduced-eye phenotype caused by overexpression of Eiger (Figure 3—figure supplement 2M–O, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 2P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 dramatically enhanced the reduced-eye phenotype caused by overexpression of Eiger.
source: Notably, although overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 alone in the eyes had no significant effect on eye morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I–K, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 2L), they dramatically enhanced the reduced-eye phenotype caused by overexpression of Eiger (Figure 3—figure supplement 2M–O, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 2P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The severity of the reduced-eye phenotype depends on the levels of JNK activation and subsequent cell death.
source: It has been shown that the severity of the reduced-eye phenotype depends on the levels of JNK activation and subsequent cell death (Igaki et al., 2002; Igaki et al., 2006; Igaki et al., 2009), suggesting that miR-306 and miR-79 enhance Eiger-mediated activation of JNK signaling.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 enhance Eiger-mediated activation of JNK signaling.
source: It has been shown that the severity of the reduced-eye phenotype depends on the levels of JNK activation and subsequent cell death (Igaki et al., 2002; Igaki et al., 2006; Igaki et al., 2009), suggesting that miR-306 and miR-79 enhance Eiger-mediated activation of JNK signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these miRNAs enhance the Eiger-induced reduced-eye phenotype.

claim: Blocking JNK signaling by overexpression of a dominant-negative form of Drosophila JNK Basket (BskDN) canceled the tumor-suppressive activity of miR-306 or miR-79 against RasV12/dlg-/- or RasV12/lgl-/- tumors.
source: Indeed, blocking JNK signaling by overexpression of a dominant-negative form of Drosophila JNK Basket (BskDN) canceled the tumor-suppressive activity of miR-306 or miR-79 against RasV12/dlg-/- or RasV12/lgl-/- tumors (Figure 3R–W, quantified in Figure 3X, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), while BskDN did not affect growth of normal tissues (Figure 3Q compare to Figure 3A, quantified in Figure 3X).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: BskDN did not affect growth of normal tissues.
source: Indeed, blocking JNK signaling by overexpression of a dominant-negative form of Drosophila JNK Basket (BskDN) canceled the tumor-suppressive activity of miR-306 or miR-79 against RasV12/dlg-/- or RasV12/lgl-/- tumors (Figure 3R–W, quantified in Figure 3X, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), while BskDN did not affect growth of normal tissues (Figure 3Q compare to Figure 3A, quantified in Figure 3X).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of BskDN significantly increased the size of dlg-/- or lgl-/- clones overexpressing miR-306 or miR-79.
source: Moreover, overexpression of BskDN significantly increased the size of dlg-/- or lgl-/- clones overexpressing miR-306 or miR-79 (Figure 3H, J, K, Y, Z, and AA, quantified in Figure 3AB; Figure 3—figure supplement 3E–J, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 suppress growth of malignant tumors by enhancing JNK signaling activation.
source: Together, these data suggest that miR-306 and miR-79 suppress growth of malignant tumors by enhancing JNK signaling activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking JNK cancels the tumor-suppressive effects of these miRNAs.

claim: Overexpression of an activated form of the Drosophila PDGF/VEGF receptor homolog (PVRact) results in JNK activation and tumor formation in the wing disc.
source: Overexpression of an activated form of the Drosophila PDGF/VEGF receptor homolog (PVRact) results in JNK activation and tumor formation in the wing disc (Wang et al., 2016a) and eye-antennal disc (Figure 4B, compare to Figure 4A, quantified in Figure 4F).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: PVRact-induced tumor growth was significantly suppressed by overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79.
source: This tumor growth was significantly suppressed by overexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 (Figure 4B–E, quantified in Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-F.

claim: Clones overexpressing the oncogene Src64B in the eye-antennal disc activate JNK signaling.
source: In addition, the size of clones overexpressing the oncogene Src64B in the eye-antennal disc (Figure 4H, compare to Figure 4G, quantified in Figure 4F), which activate JNK signaling (Enomoto and Igaki, 2013), was significantly reduced when the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 was coexpressed (Figure 4H–K, quantified in Figure 4L).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The size of Src64B-overexpressing clones was significantly reduced when the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 was coexpressed.
source: In addition, the size of clones overexpressing the oncogene Src64B in the eye-antennal disc (Figure 4H, compare to Figure 4G, quantified in Figure 4F), which activate JNK signaling (Enomoto and Igaki, 2013), was significantly reduced when the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 was coexpressed (Figure 4H–K, quantified in Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H-L.

claim: Nonautonomous overgrowth of surrounding wild-type tissue by Src64B-overexpressing clones was significantly suppressed by coexpression of the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79.
source: Moreover, nonautonomous overgrowth of surrounding wild-type tissue by Src64B-overexpressing clones (Enomoto and Igaki, 2013) was significantly suppressed by coexpression of these miRNAs (Figure 4M–P, quantified in Figure 4Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4M-Q.

claim: The size of clones mutant for RNA helicase Hel25E was significantly reduced when the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 was coexpressed.
source: Furthermore, the size of clones mutant for an RNA helicase Hel25E or an adaptor protein Mahj, both of which are eliminated by JNK-dependent cell competition when surrounded by wild-type cells (Nagata et al., 2019; Tamori et al., 2010), was significantly reduced when these miRNAs were coexpressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D, quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–I, quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The size of clones mutant for adaptor protein Mahj was significantly reduced when the miR-9c/306/79/9b cluster, miR-306, or miR-79 was coexpressed.
source: Furthermore, the size of clones mutant for an RNA helicase Hel25E or an adaptor protein Mahj, both of which are eliminated by JNK-dependent cell competition when surrounded by wild-type cells (Nagata et al., 2019; Tamori et al., 2010), was significantly reduced when these miRNAs were coexpressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D, quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–I, quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Clones mutant for Hel25E or Mahj are eliminated by JNK-dependent cell competition when surrounded by wild-type cells.
source: Furthermore, the size of clones mutant for an RNA helicase Hel25E or an adaptor protein Mahj, both of which are eliminated by JNK-dependent cell competition when surrounded by wild-type cells (Nagata et al., 2019; Tamori et al., 2010), was significantly reduced when these miRNAs were coexpressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D, quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–I, quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ectopic expression of miR-306 or miR-79 enhanced JNK activity in various tumor and cell competition models.
source: In these tumors or cell competition models, ectopic expression of miR-306 or miR-79 enhanced JNK activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Knocking down Hep using the pnr-GAL4 driver generates a split-thorax phenotype caused by reduced JNK signaling.
source: Knocking down Hep, the Drosophila JNK kinase, using the pnr-GAL4 driver generates a split-thorax phenotype caused by reduced JNK signaling (Ishimaru et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hep or Eiger using pnr-GAL4 generates a small-scutellum phenotype caused by elevated JNK signaling.
source: On the contrary, ectopic expression of Hep or Eiger using pnr-GAL4 generates a small-scutellum phenotype caused by elevated JNK signaling (Ma et al., 2013; Xue et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ectopic expression of miR-306 or miR-79 using pnr-GAL4 resulted in a small-scutellum phenotype.
source: Similarly to Hep or Eiger, ectopic expression of miR-306 or miR-79 using pnr-GAL4 resulted in a small-scutellum phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C, quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 broadly enhance JNK signaling activity stimulated by different upstream signaling.
source: These data suggest that miR-306 and miR-79 broadly enhance JNK signaling activity stimulated by different upstream signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these miRNAs enhance JNK activity in multiple different tumor models.

claim: Clustered miRNAs often target overlapping sets of genes and co-regulate various biological processes.
source: The clustered miRNAs often target overlapping sets of genes and thus co-regulate various biological processes (Kim et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2016b; Yuan et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 11 mRNAs were predicted to be targets of both miR-306 and miR-79 using TargetScanFly 7.2.
source: Given that miR-306 and miR-79 are located on the same miRNA cluster, we searched for the common targets of these miRNAs using the online software TargeyScanFly 7.2 (http://www.targetscan.org/fly_72/) and found 11 mRNAs that were predicted to be targets of both miR-306 and miR-79 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction using TargetScanFly software.

claim: Knocking down RNF146 resulted in JNK activation in Drosophila wing discs.
source: As a result, we found that knocking down of RNF146, but not any other available RNAis for the candidate genes, resulted in JNK activation (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The RNF146 mRNA has putative target sites of miR-306 and miR-79 in its 3'UTR region.
source: The RNF146 mRNA had putative target sites of miR-306 and miR-79 in its 3′UTR region (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D based on sequence analysis.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 reduced wild-type RNF146 3'UTR expression but did not affect respective mutant RNF146 3'UTR in dual-luciferase reporter assays.
source: We found that miR-306 and miR-79 reduced wild-type RNF146 3′UTR expression but did not affect respective mutant RNF146 3′UTR (Figure 5E), indicating that miR-306 and miR-79 directly target RNF146 3′UTR (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dual-luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 directly target RNF146 3'UTR.
source: We found that miR-306 and miR-79 reduced wild-type RNF146 3′UTR expression but did not affect respective mutant RNF146 3′UTR (Figure 5E), indicating that miR-306 and miR-79 directly target RNF146 3′UTR (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the dual-luciferase reporter assay results.

claim: Overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 reduced the endogenous levels of RNF146 protein.
source: We also confirmed that overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 reduced the endogenous levels of RNF146 protein (Figure 5F, quantified in Figure 5G) and that suppression of miR-306 and miR-79 functions by using miRNA sponges increased the endogenous levels of RNF146 protein in the adult eyes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Suppression of miR-306 and miR-79 functions by using miRNA sponges increased the endogenous levels of RNF146 protein in the adult eyes.
source: We also confirmed that overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 reduced the endogenous levels of RNF146 protein (Figure 5F, quantified in Figure 5G) and that suppression of miR-306 and miR-79 functions by using miRNA sponges increased the endogenous levels of RNF146 protein in the adult eyes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Knockdown of RNF146 did not affect normal tissue growth.
source: We found that, while knockdown of RNF146 did not affect normal tissue growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4C), it significantly suppressed RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth (Figure 5H–J, quantified in Figure 5K) and promoted elimination of dlg-/- clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 4D and E, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Knockdown of RNF146 significantly suppressed RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth.
source: We found that, while knockdown of RNF146 did not affect normal tissue growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4C), it significantly suppressed RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth (Figure 5H–J, quantified in Figure 5K) and promoted elimination of dlg-/- clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 4D and E, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H-K.

claim: Knockdown of RNF146 promoted elimination of dlg-/- clones.
source: We found that, while knockdown of RNF146 did not affect normal tissue growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4C), it significantly suppressed RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth (Figure 5H–J, quantified in Figure 5K) and promoted elimination of dlg-/- clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 4D and E, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of one copy of miR-306 or miR-79 in the eyes had no significant effect on the number of dying cells or eye morphology.
source: Although overexpression of one copy of miR-306 or miR-79 in the eyes had no significant effect on the number of dying cells or eye morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I–K, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 2L, Figure 5—figure supplement 4G–J, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4N), overexpression of 2×miR-306 or 2×miR-79 in the eyes significantly increased the number of dying cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 4K–M, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4N) and resulted in a reduced-eye phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 4O and Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of 2×miR-306 or 2×miR-79 in the eyes significantly increased the number of dying cells.
source: Although overexpression of one copy of miR-306 or miR-79 in the eyes had no significant effect on the number of dying cells or eye morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I–K, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 2L, Figure 5—figure supplement 4G–J, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4N), overexpression of 2×miR-306 or 2×miR-79 in the eyes significantly increased the number of dying cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 4K–M, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4N) and resulted in a reduced-eye phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 4O and Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of 2×miR-306 or 2×miR-79 in the eyes resulted in a reduced-eye phenotype.
source: Although overexpression of one copy of miR-306 or miR-79 in the eyes had no significant effect on the number of dying cells or eye morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I–K, quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 2L, Figure 5—figure supplement 4G–J, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4N), overexpression of 2×miR-306 or 2×miR-79 in the eyes significantly increased the number of dying cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 4K–M, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4N) and resulted in a reduced-eye phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 4O and Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of RNF146 rescued the reduced-eye phenotype caused by overexpression of 2×miR-306 or 2×miR-79 in the eyes.
source: Overexpression of RNF146 rescued the reduced-eye phenotype caused by overexpression of 2×miR-306 or 2×miR-79 in the eyes (Figure 5—figure supplement 4O–R, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4S).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Knocking down RNF146 significantly enhanced Eiger-induced reduced-eye phenotype.
source: Moreover, knocking down of RNF146 significantly enhanced Eiger-induced reduced-eye phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 4T–W, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4X).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of RNF146 did not affect RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth.
source: Furthermore, although overexpression of RNF146 did not affect RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth (Figure 5L–M, quantified in Figure 5N), overexpression of RNF146 weakened the tumor-suppressive effect of miR-306 or miR-79 on RasV12/dlg-/- tumors (Figure 5O–R, quantified in Figure 5S).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5L-N.

claim: Overexpression of RNF146 weakened the tumor-suppressive effect of miR-306 or miR-79 on RasV12/dlg-/- tumors.
source: Furthermore, although overexpression of RNF146 did not affect RasV12/dlg-/- tumor growth (Figure 5L–M, quantified in Figure 5N), overexpression of RNF146 weakened the tumor-suppressive effect of miR-306 or miR-79 on RasV12/dlg-/- tumors (Figure 5O–R, quantified in Figure 5S).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5O-S.

claim: RNF146 overexpression weakened the enhanced elimination of dlg-/- clones by miR-306 or miR-79.
source: The RNF146 overexpression also weakened the enhanced elimination of dlg-/- clones by miR-306 or miR-79 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4Y–AB, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 4AC).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Knocking down RNF146 enhanced JNK activity in RasV12/dlg-/- tumors.
source: Similarly to ectopic expression of miR-306 or miR-79, knocking down of RNF146 enhanced JNK activity in RasV12/dlg-/- tumors (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A and B, quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 directly target RNF146 mRNA, thereby enhancing JNK signaling activity and exerting tumor-suppressive effects.
source: Together, these data indicate that miR-306 and miR-79 directly target RNF146 mRNA, thereby enhancing JNK signaling activity and thus exerting the tumor-suppressive effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental data showing direct targeting and functional consequences.

claim: Loss of RNF146 upregulates the protein levels of Tnks in Drosophila embryos, larvae, wing discs, and adult eyes.
source: It has been shown in Drosophila embryos, larvae, wing discs, and adult eyes that loss of RNF146 upregulates the protein levels of Tnks (Gultekin and Steller, 2019; Wang et al., 2019), a poly-ADP-ribose polymerase that directly mediates poly-ADP ribosylation of JNK, which triggers K63-linked poly-ubiquitination of JNK and thereby promotes JNK-dependent apoptosis in Drosophila (Feng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tnks is a poly-ADP-ribose polymerase that directly mediates poly-ADP ribosylation of JNK.
source: It has been shown in Drosophila embryos, larvae, wing discs, and adult eyes that loss of RNF146 upregulates the protein levels of Tnks (Gultekin and Steller, 2019; Wang et al., 2019), a poly-ADP-ribose polymerase that directly mediates poly-ADP ribosylation of JNK, which triggers K63-linked poly-ubiquitination of JNK and thereby promotes JNK-dependent apoptosis in Drosophila (Feng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Poly-ADP ribosylation of JNK triggers K63-linked poly-ubiquitination of JNK and promotes JNK-dependent apoptosis in Drosophila.
source: It has been shown in Drosophila embryos, larvae, wing discs, and adult eyes that loss of RNF146 upregulates the protein levels of Tnks (Gultekin and Steller, 2019; Wang et al., 2019), a poly-ADP-ribose polymerase that directly mediates poly-ADP ribosylation of JNK, which triggers K63-linked poly-ubiquitination of JNK and thereby promotes JNK-dependent apoptosis in Drosophila (Feng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of RNF146 enhanced rough-eye phenotype caused by Tnks overexpression.
source: In addition, loss of RNF146 was shown to enhance rough-eye phenotype caused by Tnks overexpression (Gultekin and Steller, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of Tnks induces phosphorylation of JNK (JNK activation) in S2 cells.
source: Indeed, as reported previously (Feng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018), Western blot analysis revealed that overexpression of Tnks induces phosphorylation of JNK (JNK activation) in S2 cells (Figure 6A, lane 2 vs. lane 1, quantified in Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A and 6C, and by citations to previous literature.

claim: Coexpression of RNF146 significantly downregulated Tnks protein level and suppressed Tnks-induced JNK phosphorylation in S2 cells.
source: Notably, coexpression of RNF146 significantly downregulated Tnks protein level and suppressed Tnks-induced JNK phosphorylation (Figure 6A, lane 3 vs. lane 2, quantified in Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Knocking down RNF146 significantly upregulated Tnks protein level and promoted JNK phosphorylation in S2 cells.
source: Moreover, knocking down of RNF146 or overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 significantly upregulated Tnks protein level and promoted JNK phosphorylation (Figure 6D, quantified in Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, quantified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 significantly upregulated Tnks protein level and promoted JNK phosphorylation in S2 cells.
source: Moreover, knocking down of RNF146 or overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 significantly upregulated Tnks protein level and promoted JNK phosphorylation (Figure 6D, quantified in Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, quantified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Downregulation of RNF146 or overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 enhances JNK activation via upregulation of Tnks.
source: These data support the notion that downregulation of RNF146 or overexpression of miR-306 or miR-79 enhances JNK activation via upregulation of Tnks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Western blot data showing upregulation of Tnks and JNK phosphorylation.

claim: Overexpression of Tnks was sufficient to suppress growth of either normal tissues or RasV12/dlg-/- tumors.
source: Indeed, overexpression of Tnks was sufficient to suppress growth of either normal tissues or RasV12/dlg-/- tumors (Figure 6G–J, quantified in Figure 6K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G-K.

claim: Tnks suppresses growth of RasV12/dlg-/- tumors by cooperating with JNK signaling.
source: Due to the fact that overexpression of Tnks alone resulted in larger clone size than RasV12/dlg-/-+Tnks clone (Figure 6H and J, quantified in Figure 6K), our data support the notion that Tnks suppresses growth of RasV12/dlg-/- tumors by cooperating with JNK signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Tnks has a stronger suppressive effect in tumors than in normal tissue.

claim: Overexpression of Tnks rescued the lethality of flies bearing RasV12/dlg-/- tumors in the eye-antennal discs.
source: Consistent with the data shown above, overexpression of Tnks rescued the lethality of flies bearing RasV12/dlg-/- tumors in the eye-antennal discs (Figure 6L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6L and M.

claim: Tnks protein levels were significantly higher in Rnf146 mutant background than in wild-type.
source: A pervious study has shown that Tnks protein levels were significantly higher in Rnf146 mutant background than in wild-type (Gultekin and Steller, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Blocking new protein synthesis in S2 cells by cycloheximide resulted in a time-dependent depletion of Tnks protein with a half-life of less than 3 hr.
source: Blocking new protein synthesis in S2 cells by the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX) resulted in a time-dependent depletion of Tnks protein with a half-life of less than 3 hr (Figure 6N, quantified in Figure 6P).
evidence: This claim is supported by cycloheximide chase experiment data shown in Figure 6N and P.

claim: Depletion of Tnks was significantly retarded when RNF146 was knocked down.
source: This depletion of Tnks was significantly retarded when RNF146 was knocked down (Figure 6O, quantified in Figure 6P).
evidence: This claim is supported by cycloheximide chase experiment data shown in Figure 6O and P.

claim: Endogenous RNF146 promotes degradation of Tnks protein.
source: These data indicate that endogenous RNF146 promotes degradation of Tnks protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cycloheximide chase experiments showing retarded Tnks degradation when RNF146 is knocked down.

claim: miR-306 or miR-79 directly targets RNF146, leading to elevation of Tnks protein that induces noncanonical activation of JNK signaling.
source: Taken together, our data show that miR-306 or miR-79 directly targets RNF146, thereby leading to elevation of Tnks protein that induces noncanonical activation of JNK signaling (Figure 6Q).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: This noncanonical mode of JNK activation has only a weak effect on normal tissue growth but strongly blocks tumor growth by overactivating JNK signaling when tumors already possess elevated JNK signaling via the canonical JNK pathway.
source: Importantly, this noncanonical mode of JNK activation has only a weak effect on normal tissue growth but it strongly blocks tumor growth by overactivating JNK signaling when tumors already possess elevated JNK signaling via the canonical JNK pathway (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental data showing differential effects in normal vs. tumor tissue.

claim: Tumors or premalignant mutant cells often activate canonical JNK signaling.
source: Given that tumors or premalignant mutant cells often activate canonical JNK signaling, miR-306 and miR-79 can be novel ideal targets of cancer therapy.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and the experimental observations in the study.

claim: miR-306 and miR-79 can be novel ideal targets of cancer therapy.
source: Given that tumors or premalignant mutant cells often activate canonical JNK signaling, miR-306 and miR-79 can be novel ideal targets of cancer therapy.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Atf3 encodes an AP-1 transcription factor that is a polarity-loss responsive gene acting downstream of the membrane-associated Scrib polarity complex.
source: Atf3 encodes an AP-1 transcription factor that was shown to be a polarity-loss responsive gene acting downstream of the membrane-associated Scrib polarity complex (Donohoe et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of Atf3 suppresses growth and invasion of RasV12/scrib-/- tumors in eye-antennal discs.
source: Knockdown of Atf3 suppresses growth and invasion of RasV12/scrib-/- tumors in eye-antennal discs (Atkins et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Chinmo is a BTB-zinc finger oncogene that is upregulated by JNK signaling in tumors.
source: Chinmo is a BTB-zinc finger oncogene that is upregulated by JNK signaling in tumors (Doggett et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Loss of chinmo does not significantly suppress tumor growth.
source: Although loss of chinmo does not significantly suppress tumor growth, overexpression of chinmo with RasV12 or an activated Notch is sufficient to promote tumor growth in eye-antennal discs (Doggett et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of chinmo with RasV12 or an activated Notch is sufficient to promote tumor growth in eye-antennal discs.
source: Although loss of chinmo does not significantly suppress tumor growth, overexpression of chinmo with RasV12 or an activated Notch is sufficient to promote tumor growth in eye-antennal discs (Doggett et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Chn encodes a zinc finger transcription factor that cooperates with scrib-/- to promote tumor growth.
source: Chn encodes a zinc finger transcription factor that cooperates with scrib-/- to promote tumor growth (Turkel et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of Atf3, chinmo, or chn did not activate JNK signaling.
source: Although we found that knockdown of these genes did not activate JNK signaling, it is possible that these putative target genes also contribute to the miR-306/miR-79-induced tumor suppression.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations in the study.

claim: It is possible that Atf3, chinmo, and chn also contribute to miR-306/miR-79-induced tumor suppression.
source: Although we found that knockdown of these genes did not activate JNK signaling, it is possible that these putative target genes also contribute to the miR-306/miR-79-induced tumor suppression.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the fact that these genes are predicted targets.

claim: miR-79 is downregulated in RasV12/lgl-RNAi tumors in Drosophila wing discs.
source: Intriguingly, it has been reported that miR-79 is downregulated in RasV12/lgl-RNAi tumors in Drosophila wing discs (Shu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: It is highly possible that miR-306 is also downregulated in tumors.
source: Given that miR-306 is located in the same miRNA cluster with miR-79, it is highly possible that miR-306 is also downregulated in tumors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that miR-306 and miR-79 are clustered together.

claim: Tumors have mechanisms that downregulate antitumor miRNAs for their survival and growth.
source: This suggests that tumors have the mechanism that downregulates antitumor miRNAs for their survival and growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that miR-79 is downregulated in tumors.

claim: miR-9, the mammalian homolog of miR-79, is predicted to target mammalian RNF146.
source: Considering that miR-9, the mammalian homolog of miR-79, is predicted to target mammalian RNF146 (Figure 5—figure supplement 6) and that JNK signaling is highly conserved throughout evolution, it opens up the possibility of developing a new miRNA-based strategy against cancer.
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction shown in the referenced figure.

claim: JNK signaling is highly conserved throughout evolution.
source: Considering that miR-9, the mammalian homolog of miR-79, is predicted to target mammalian RNF146 (Figure 5—figure supplement 6) and that JNK signaling is highly conserved throughout evolution, it opens up the possibility of developing a new miRNA-based strategy against cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about JNK signaling.

claim: The findings open up the possibility of developing a new miRNA-based strategy against cancer.
source: Considering that miR-9, the mammalian homolog of miR-79, is predicted to target mammalian RNF146 (Figure 5—figure supplement 6) and that JNK signaling is highly conserved throughout evolution, it opens up the possibility of developing a new miRNA-based strategy against cancer.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings and evolutionary conservation.
